newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: De Beers annual results expected to dazzle.
newsitem.headline: De Beers annual results expected to dazzle.

text.p: Diamond giant De Beers Ltd is set to cut a polished set of year results next Tuesday as rising gem sales and its extensive portfolio of investments reaps healthy profits, analysts said.
The firm posted good interim figures last August and little change is seen to a positive trend in diamond sales and benefits from large holdings in other firms like Anglo American and Minorco .
"The diamond sales, the depreciation of the rand and the investment companies should all be good," said Ross Gardiner, analyst at SocGen Frankel Pollak.
Analysts see a total earnings per share of 11.97-14.00 rand, against 9.38 rand last time and a dividend of 370 to 447 cents a share, up from 339 cents.

Demand for diamonds has been good with De Beers selling record amounts by value. Analysts said they would be looking for encouraging signs of demand in the lucrative Japanese and South East Asia markets.
However, while diamonds may be forever, De Beers has discovered that cartels are not.
The firm, which sells about 75 percent of the world's diamond production through its London-based Central Selling Organisation, has had contract rows with Australia and Russia.
Analysts said the firm's comments on these areas, and in Canada where Australia's Broken Hill is considering selling outside the CSO, would be watched for hints of trends in the whole industry.
Last year Australia's CRA Ltd said its open cut Argyle mine, the world's biggest diamond mine, would snub the CSO and market its gems directly.
Russia, however, looks more likely to stay with De Beers once a new marketing contract is signed.
Russian monopoly diamond producer Almazy Rossii-Sakha is currently outside the De Beers system after it missed a New Year's Eve deadline to sign a new deal.
But recently Interfax news agency quoted Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Vladimir Potanin as saying a deal was likely to be signed soon.

Analysts agreed, saying that De Beers had called Russia's bluff. "The Russians could have kept them running around for ever. Ending the deal called their bluff and concentrated their minds," one analyst said.

However, despite the apparent break-up of much of the cartel De Beers shares have rocketed recently to near record highs. At 0910 GMT they were at 157.25 rand after touching 121.75 rand as recently as December 19.
The market is expecting the shares to trend higher yet. "They are moving upwards and could go higher," Gardiner said.
Analysts said the market now saw the firm more in terms of a markting group, not a production cartel. "The firm is becoming more a marketing machine than a cartel of production," one analyst said.

One possible area of concern for De Beers and the global diamond industry is a flood of cheap diamonds plucked from the river beds of northern Angola. The area is largely controlled by local warlords and production costs are cheap.

Analysts said, however, that the problem would be a short-term one as the alluvial deposits were set to run out over the next four years and the country would need the help of big firms to mine its remaining diamond reserves.

De Beers, which pioneered much of the river bed exploration befre having to leave the country as banditry escalated inthe war-torn country, could then re-enter with more conventional mining operations, analysts said.
